captions: GroundTruth. The ground knows what day it is.
Seismometers were built to hear earthquakes.
They also hear us: buses, trains, machinery and footsteps.
So can a computer read the day of the week from the ground alone?
The site opens on the Earth, in the real night sky.
NASA Blue Marble imagery and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue
Along the bottom, a pen draws one real day under Brussels.
An average Wednesday before the 2020 lockdown
Scroll, and the pen draws the day hour by hour.
Almost still at night. Then the city wakes up.
A Sunday has no morning cliff.
Only people keep office hours
Ask the ground: any of 33 cities, any day since 2019.
Christmas Day 2019 in Brussels was a Wednesday.
The model only sees that one day of shaking, never the date
It reads like a Sunday.
Every answer comes from a model that never trained on that week
The year, one column per week: the weekends show up as blue bands.
Ascension Day, a Thursday: also read as a Sunday.
Weekday holidays read as a weekend 67% of the time, ordinary weekdays 1.5%
March 2020. One line per city, sorted by the day it went quiet.
Blue means at least 15% quieter than usual.
Each city against its own previous eight weeks
The globe: 33 cities, every day since January 2019.
Play through March 2020 and the cities turn blue as lockdowns begin.
Every day, a GitHub Action scores yesterday for 7 live cities.
Days the model never trained on
18 predictions were written down before their day, then graded automatically.
